scores.evidence: CRDTs are easier for offline support and peer-to-peer. The cost is metadata growth.
scores.rationale: Generally correct statements (idempotent updates, state vectors, relative-position anchoring, IME risk) but shallow and doesn't reach hard parts like rich-text merge semantics or durability-before-ack.

scores.evidence: Rich text with blocks is the usual target.
scores.rationale: Covers the main capabilities and a buildable sequence, but defers the core choices and never fixes scope or states exclusions with reasons.

scores.evidence: Route each document to one server instance, or use a pub/sub layer such as Redis so multiple servers can share a document.
scores.rationale: Recognizable phased design, but it is a menu of alternatives with no committed architecture and unclear data ownership; local persistence plus 'plain save endpoint' sits awkwardly with sync.

scores.evidence: Write convergence tests. Run randomized concurrent edits against the model and check that all replicas end up identical.
scores.rationale: Convergence tests are early and domain-appropriate, and load/soak tests exist, but no measurable criteria, no duplicate/reorder specifics, and no production validation.

scores.evidence: Set non-functional targets. These are the maximum concurrent editors per document, the latency budget (typically under 100 ms perceived)
scores.rationale: Identifies unspecified constraints as items to decide and ends by asking for stack, team and offline needs, but states no actual assumptions or sensitivity.

scores.evidence: Security: rate limiting, input and update validation, payload size caps, and protection against malicious or malformed updates.
scores.rationale: Failures are mentioned as list items late in hardening (malicious updates, flaky networks, IME) with little detection or recovery, and crash or corruption handling is absent.

scores.evidence: Observability: metrics for sync latency, connection counts, and update sizes, plus error tracking.
scores.rationale: Metrics and backups/DR drills are named, but there is no deployment, rollback, migration, alerting or ownership plan.
Costs are not discussed at all, including build-vs-buy, infrastructure or scaling cost.

scores.evidence: Phase 0: Decisions that are expensive to change later
scores.rationale: Explicitly flags algorithm, document model and editor framework as costly early choices, but offers no isolation, migration or exit paths and no schema versioning.

scores.evidence: Horizontal scaling, multi-region deployment, and backups and disaster recovery drills.
scores.rationale: Mostly proportionate with scale deferred to the end, but it includes a comment/suggestions, audit log, DOCX export and multi-region in one list without prioritization, and a single-user phase that is wasteful.

scores.evidence: Milestone: two browsers edit the same document and converge.
scores.rationale: Ordered phases with some milestones and a team split, but the technology choices are left open and the single-user-first ordering has a dependency problem.

checklist.evidence: Adopting an existing library is usually better than writing your own.
Build the document schema: paragraphs, headings, lists, marks, and so on.
Run randomized concurrent edits against the model and check that all replicas end up identical.
Store updates durably: an append-only log plus periodic snapshots and compaction.
Route each document to one server instance, or use a pub/sub layer such as Redis
Offline editing with a local queue, and a clear "syncing / offline / saved" indicator.
Enforce them on the WebSocket, not just in the UI.
Undo/redo scoped to each user's own changes. This is a common bug source.
Presence: who is online, with colored cursors and selections (awareness protocol).
Write convergence tests... Do this before adding features.
Load and soak tests: many clients on one document, large documents, and flaky networks.

traps.evidence: Adopting an existing library is usually better than writing your own.
Phase 1: Single-user editor (no networking)... Phase 2: Core sync engine
Store updates durably: an append-only log plus periodic snapshots and compaction.
CRDTs are easier for offline support and peer-to-peer. The cost is metadata growth.

note: A generic, sensible-sounding phase list that defers nearly every real decision, is weak on durability, failure handling, versioning and cost, and builds a single-user editor before sync.
